1:
Job opens his reply with the question that governs the whole chapter, “Why, seeing times are not hidden from the Almighty, do they that know him not see his days?” — and the witnesses read it as a perplexity raised not from his own case only but from a survey of God's dealings with the world at large. The reformed John Gill takes the premise first: since all things are appointed by God, and he punctually performs what he has decreed, the times of executing his purposes cannot be hidden from him; as there is a season set for every purpose under heaven, that season must be known to the God who fixed it, all his works being known to him from eternity. The Vulgate, Gill notes, reduces the clause to a flat proposition, “times are not hidden from the Almighty” — no sort of time, in the world or in the life of any man, escapes him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry builds the whole doctrine of omniscience out of the verb. Past times are not hidden from God's judgment (Eccl. 3:15), present times not hidden from his providence (Matt. 10:29), future times not hidden from his prescience (Acts 15:18); he governs the world and therefore takes cognizance of it, and every man's times are in his hand and under his eye. Yet those who know him — the wise and good with whom his secret is — “do not see his day,” the day of his judging for them or against notorious sinners; this was the very thing Job complained of in his own case at ch. 23:8, that he could not see God appear to plead his cause. It is a mystery of Providence, Henry allows, but there is a reason for the deferral, and God will exercise the faith and patience of his people, and stir their prayers for the coming of his kingdom, for which they are to cry day and night to him (Luke 18:7).

The wesleyan-arminian voices sharpen the demand. Adam Clarke follows Mr. Good's bolder rendering, “Wherefore are not doomsdays kept by the Almighty, so that his offenders may eye their periods?” — reading the “times” as fixed term-days of assize; God reserves the knowledge of these to himself, so that while in the aggregate the just are rewarded and the wicked punished, the exceptions are numerous enough to leave the whole scheme mysterious. John Wesley glosses the “times” as the fittest seasons for punishing wicked men, which, were they constant and fixed in this life, would not be unknown to good men, to whom God uses to reveal his secrets. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds that even those who love and serve God are as perplexed about his principles of government as those who know him not, and remarks that the ambiguity of the Authorized Version's second negative would vanish if we read “see not” rather than “not see.” The witnesses converge: the question is a real one, and Job does not so much resolve it as lay it open.
2:
From the general perplexity Job descends to particulars, and the first class of oppressors he names are those who plunder under colour of law. “Some remove the landmarks,” he charges, and the reformed John Gill explains the crime: the boundary-stones anciently set to distinguish one man's land from another and to secure property were shifted, whether secretly by night or openly by force, under pretence that they were wrongly placed. It was forbidden in the law of Moses as an accursed thing, yet it was known to be evil by the light of nature long before that law was given; even the heathen, Gill observes, had a deity they called Jupiter Terminalis set over bounds, and Numa Pompilius ordered that whoever removed them should be slain as a sacrilegious person. Some, he adds, render the verb more strictly still — “they touch the landmarks” — as though even to lay a hand on them were unlawful.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same act as the disseizing of neighbours of the real estate that came to them by descent: they remove the land-marks under pretence that they were misplaced, and so encroach and think to secure to their posterity what they have got wrongfully. This the law of Moses forbade under a curse (Deut. 19:14; Deut. 27:17); forging or destroying deeds, Henry notes, is now a crime equivalent to it. As for “they violently take away flocks, and feed thereof,” he adds that they dispossess men of their personal estate under colour of justice, taking flocks as though forfeited and pasturing them as their own.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the wording. Keil and Delitzsch render the line “They remove the landmarks, they steal flocks and shepherd them,” so that the robbers openly graze as their own the very flocks they have driven off; and they linger over the syntax of the opening question, where the construct “the times” followed by a genitive marks the point at which a man's fate is decided, comparing the day of a man's end in ch. 15:32 and ch. 18:20. Charles Ellicott agrees that the removal of landmarks was expressly provided against by the Mosaic law, and would render the second clause “feed them” rather than “feed thereof” — that is, pasture the stolen flocks, the more easily done once the boundaries are gone. Adam Clarke rounds out the philology: Mr. Good takes the verb from a root meaning to rend rather than to feed, while the Septuagint read “shepherd,” picturing the robbers as “violently carrying off both the flock and the shepherd.” The witnesses do not divide; together they set the pattern of a lawlessness that wears the mask of legal right.
3:
The second stroke of the same picture falls on the two most defenceless figures in Israel, and the witnesses hear in the paired victims a studied cruelty: “they drive away the ass of the fatherless, they take the widow's ox for a pledge.” The reformed John Gill notes that the fatherless, left destitute of any to provide for them, might own but a single ass to carry their goods or to ride upon — a creature of no great worth, yet the more cruel to drive away because it is all they have. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the same point of singleness: the ass and the ox, the fatherless and the widow, each presumably having no more than one, so that the seizure strips them bare. He observes that Job first describes the oppression of the country and then, at v.12, that of the city, and thinks we catch here a glimpse of some oppressed and servile race, haunting the desert and suffering at the hands of the more powerful tribes — man's inhumanity to man being, he says, a crime of very long standing.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the verse into a matter of God's own honour. If a poor fatherless child has but an ass to earn a little by, they find some colour to take it away; if a widow has but an ox for her little husbandry, under pretence of distraining for some small debt this ox shall be taken for a pledge, though perhaps it is the widow's all. But God, Henry reminds them, has taken it among the titles of his honour to be a Father of the fatherless and a judge of the widows; and therefore those who do not to their utmost protect and help them he will reckon with as his enemies. Cruelty to those who lie at our mercy, he adds, cries aloud for vengeance, and those who show no mercy shall themselves have judgment without mercy.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fixes the illegality of the act with a single stroke: to take the widow's ox for a pledge was contrary to God's law, written first in men's hearts and afterwards in holy Scripture at Exod. 22:26-27, which forbade even keeping a poor man's garment overnight. The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as a deliberate choice of the weakest prey — the orphan's one beast, the widow's one ox — and set against it the standing declaration of God that the fatherless and the widow are his own peculiar care, so that the oppressor's petty distraint is in truth a quarrel picked with heaven.
4:
The oppression now spills off the field and onto the road, where the poor are jostled aside by men who own the highway as they have seized the land: “they turn the needy out of the way.” The reformed John Gill ranges the senses the phrase will bear — morally, turning them out of the way of righteousness and truth by threats or flatteries; civilly, taking from them the means of their livelihood; or literally, forcing them to turn aside from the path in a supercilious and haughty manner, so that the poor, in fear, get out of the way lest they be insulted, beaten, or stripped of the little they have. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the closing clause the pathos of a whole class in hiding: they will mislead the poor if they can, banter and abuse them, turn them out of the way of getting relief, threaten to punish them as vagabonds, and force them to abscond — so that “the poor of the earth hide themselves together,” having no other way to secure themselves from such men.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the abuse a concrete face. These oppressors will not permit the poor to go by the accustomed paths but oblige them to take circuitous routes, the shutting-up of an ancient right-of-way; and he tells the story of a nobleman who closed a footpath that had existed time out of mind, and of the poor cobbler who went to law against him and won, on the ground that the way had been public beyond memory. Asked how he dared contend with so great a man, the cobbler answered only, “Because I did not like to leave the world worse than I found it” — for all tolerated oppression, Clarke concludes, and every voluntary forfeiture of ancient rights, is an injury to society, and those who wink at it leave the world worse than they found it. John Wesley reads the verse to the same effect: the needy are driven out of the very path in which these tyrants walk, and labour to keep out of their way, hiding themselves for fear of further injuries.

The witnesses do not divide over the picture. Whether the “turning out of the way” be read as moral seduction, economic ruin, or the plain insolence of shouldering a beggar off the road, they agree on the end of it — a countryside in which the poor must travel by stealth and lie hidden, banded together in their common helplessness, because the strong have made even the public way their private ground.
5:
With the fifth verse the scene shifts to the wilderness, and a real difference of reading opens beneath the imagery, for the witnesses do not agree whom Job sees ranging there like wild asses. The reformed John Gill lays out the choices: the words may describe the poor themselves, driven from their homes and forced to forage in the desert and keep the company of its wild creatures; or the note of comparison being supplied by the Targum, they may picture the wicked oppressors, likened to the untamed ass for their folly, wantonness, and lawlessness — and Gill thinks of the wild Arabs in Job's own neighbourhood, the sons of Ishmael, who lived by plunder and robbery. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke leans the same way toward a lawless, roaming band who make a predatory life their trade, frequent the wilderness, seize whatever they find, and so support themselves and their children; he thinks of the Bedouins, whom the oppression of tyrannous governors first drove into the deserts to a wandering, plundering way of life.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes them plainly as robbers, and reads the character with relish: they are as wild asses in the desert, untamed and under no restraint of law or government, of the very stamp of Ishmael in Gen. 16:12; they choose the desert that they may be lawless, and stealing is their trade — they “rise betimes for a prey,” going forth to it as a man goes forth to his honest labour in Ps. 104:23, and the wilderness yields food for them and their children as they bless themselves in the spoil without remorse. John Wesley agrees flatly: the wild asses are lawless, fierce, and greedy of prey, and the “they” are the oppressors, who go forth to spoil and rob.

So the debate is genuine, though it never becomes a quarrel: is the wilderness the refuge of the hunted poor, reduced to a beast's foraging, or the lair of the predatory wicked, ranging like wild asses after their prey? Gill and Clarke keep both readings in view; Henry and Wesley settle on the robbers. What all of them grant is that the desert sets no man beyond the reach of God's eye and hand — whether it hides a victim or shelters a thief, it is no covert from heaven, and the God who seems to overlook these lives sees every foraging of them.
6:
The robbers' harvest is a stolen one, and the witnesses read the sixth verse as the picture of men reaping where they have not sown. The reformed John Gill will not have it that the poor are reaping the wicked man's corn for hire; rather the wicked reap the corn of the poor, and so impudently that they do not steal it by night from the barn but come openly and cut it down standing in the field as if it were their own. The word, he notes, denotes a mixture of the poorer sorts of grain, scarce better than fodder for cattle, yet even this they carry off; and some ancient versions, dividing the word differently, read “which is not their own,” marking the plain injustice of the seizure. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds the verse perfectly characteristic of the marauding hordes: they make sudden irruptions, carry off the harvest of grain and vine, and plunge with it into the wilderness where none can follow; the Chaldee, he adds, reads that “they reap in a field that is not their own, and cut off the vineyard of the wicked.”

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would resolve the odd phrase “the vintage of the wicked” by taking the corn and the vintage to be the rich tyrant's own: while these labourers reap his corn and gather his provender, they are left to go hungry themselves. Keil and Delitzsch set the verse in the running catalogue of wrongs that stretches to v.12, reading it of the drudgery imposed on the stripped and defrauded poor, who work another's fields and presses without share in the produce. John Wesley alone turns the phrase against the robbers in a grimmer key: the corn and the vintage are those of men as wicked as themselves, so that they rob promiscuously, plundering even their brethren in iniquity.

Beneath the agreement runs a quiet fork of reading. Is the “vintage of the wicked” the spoil that one wicked man wrests from another — the spoiler himself spoiled, as Gill and Wesley half-suggest — or is it the tyrant's own crop, gathered by hands he leaves unfed, as Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch prefer? The witnesses do not press the difference to a breach. They agree on the essential scandal: a harvest changing hands by violence, and men reaping in security what they have no right to reap, while those who did the sowing and the labour stand by empty.
7:
“They cause the naked to lodge without clothing, that they have no covering in the cold” — and the witnesses divide, gently, over whether the naked here are the oppressor's victims or the wandering poor themselves. The reformed John Gill reads them as the plundered: men already poorly clothed and thinly arrayed, having scarce anything but rags, from whom the wicked take even the bed-clothes — for it is these, Gill thinks, that are chiefly meant — so that they are forced to lie all night long without a covering against the cold. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke would rather render it “they spend the night naked, without clothing,” and takes it as another trait of the wandering Arab hordes, who are ill-fed, ill-clothed, and often too impoverished even for tents, and who, living by plunder, must flee at a moment's notice and cannot encumber themselves with more than bare necessity.

The difference is real but quiet: on Gill's reading the nakedness is a wound inflicted by the strong, on Clarke's it is the hard estate of the marauders who inflict wounds elsewhere. Yet both come to the same shivering picture, and neither will let the cold be softened into metaphor. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps to the victims and heightens the outrage: the robbers cause those they have stripped, not leaving them so much as the clothes to their backs, to lodge in the cold nights without clothing; and he remembers that Eliphaz had charged Job himself with just such inhumanity, stripping the naked of their clothing, in ch. 22:6 — whereas here are men truly guilty of it who yet go unpunished. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees in a phrase: the naked are those whom the oppressors have stripped of their garments and coverings, left to the night with nothing to shield them.

The witnesses draw the same moral from the bare fact. It is the cruelty of a settled system, not a single act of passion, that leaves a man to lie down under the open sky with nothing on him — the very garment taken in pledge that the law of Exod. 22:26-27 commanded to be restored before nightfall, that the poor might sleep and not curse his creditor. Whether the sufferer be the stripped tenant of Gill, Henry, and Wesley or the desert-dweller of Clarke, the scandal Job presses is the same: that such misery lies open to every eye, and yet, as the chapter keeps insisting, God seems for the present to lay no folly to those who cause it.
8:
The night without a covering becomes a night out in the weather, and the witnesses follow the naked poor to the one shelter left them, the bare face of the rock. The reformed John Gill pictures them lying at the foot of a hill, where the clouds gather and break, or where the snow upon the height melts and runs down in streams, so that the ill-clothed are drenched with the showers of the mountains, wet as Nebuchadnezzar's body was with the dew of heaven when he was driven from men. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, who had seen such storms in mountainous country, defends the Authorized rendering against Mr. Good's “torrents”: “showers of the mountain” is strictly proper, for he has watched the tails of water-spouts intercepted and broken on the peaks, pouring down in a violence that scoops gullies from the hillsides; and in such a deluge the firm rock is the only shelter that can be found or safely trusted, which is why the poor “embrace the rock for want of a shelter.”

John Wesley reads the verse the same way and adds the detail that completes it: they are wet with the rain-water that runs down the rocks and mountains into the caves to which they have fled, and are glad when they can find a cleft in the rock in which to gain some little protection against the weather. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, expounding the whole passage of the hunted poor, sees them driven to embrace the rock for want of a better shelter, glad of a cave or den to preserve them from the injuries of the storm; and he presses the point Job is really making — that there are men truly guilty of the very cruelties Eliphaz had falsely laid to Job's charge, and yet they prosper, the curse they lie under working invisibly. Job thinks it more just, Henry observes, to argue from an open and notorious course of wickedness to a secret and future punishment, than to do as Eliphaz did and infer, from nothing but present trouble, a course of past secret iniquity.

The witnesses do not divide. They dwell on the image because it is so pitiably exact — a human creature clinging to cold stone under a mountain downpour, with no roof but the cliff and no covering but the rain — and they let it stand as Job means it to stand, an open and unanswered spectacle of misery, the sort of suffering that ought, on the friends' theology, to be met by some visible stroke against the oppressor, and is not.
9:
The catalogue of cruelties reaches its most inhuman point, and the witnesses recoil with Job at men who “pluck the fatherless from the breast.” The reformed John Gill weighs the possible motives, each worse than the last: they tear the infant away to starve it, or to sell it into slavery, or to force the mother to wean it before its time that she may be the fitter for their work; and he records Broughton's rendering, “of mischievousness they rob the fatherless,” as though the deed sprang from the greatness of the mischief, or from the exceeding mischievous disposition of men to whom cruelty is a pleasure. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it of oppressors under despotic rule who forcibly take young children to bring them up in bondage; and the second clause, “they take a pledge of the poor,” he applies to grasping landlords who let their ground at an exorbitant rent and, when the diligent labourer still cannot pay, sell him up or seize his cow, his horse, his cart, or his very bed in pledge — one of the crying sins, Clarke adds, of whole countries of Europe.

John Wesley keeps to the sharpest sense of the first clause: out of pure covetousness they will not allow the mother even the time to suckle her infant, but pluck it from her to set her to their service. The three readings differ only in the shade of the motive — murder, traffic, or greed — and agree in the horror; there is no gentler way, the witnesses imply, to take an interpretation of so brutal a line.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into his wider indictment of oppression under colour of law. Having made poor children fatherless, he says, these men make them motherless too, breaking the mother's heart when they have taken the father's life, and so starving the little ones; Pharaoh and Herod, he remembers, plucked children from the breast to the sword, and we read of little ones brought forth to the murderers in Hos. 9:13 — inhuman murderers indeed, that can with such pleasure suck innocent blood. To take a pledge of the poor is to rob the very hospital; nay, to take the poor themselves for a pledge, as some read it, distraining them for slaves after the manner of Neh. 5:5, is great wickedness that cries aloud for vengeance, and those who show no mercy to such as lie at their mercy shall themselves have judgment without mercy. The witnesses do not divide; they let the verse stand as the nadir of the chapter's cruelty, an outrage done to the most helpless of all, and unpunished.
10:
The tenth verse returns to the stripped and the starving, and the witnesses feel the bitter irony that runs through it — men made to “go naked without clothing” while their own hands carry another's harvest. The reformed John Gill reads it of the labourer whose raiment has been taken for a pledge, or whose wages are withheld so that he cannot buy so much as a covering, and is therefore driven to go naked, or next to it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens both clauses: the oppressors seize the very cloth made for the family's wear, or the wool and flax out of which it should be made, and they take away the sheaf as soon as it is reaped, snatching the grain to pay themselves their exorbitant rent, so that the ricks which should have fed the household are carried off from the hungry.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the wording and its deliberate paradox. Charles Ellicott would render the clause so that the poor “go about naked without clothing,” and “an hungered they carry the sheaves” — the tautology, meaningless in English, being expressive in the Hebrew, which sets the labourer's own nakedness beside the abundance he bears on his shoulders for his master. Keil and Delitzsch expound the same picture of forced and unrewarded toil, the stripped and famished poor bearing in the sheaves of the very men who have stripped and famished them; the whole turn of the passage, on their reading, is the deliberate pairing of the labourer's want with the harvest he gathers for another, so that his service is the measure of his misery.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the injustice with a homely comparison: those masters forget that they have a Master in heaven who will not allow the necessary supports of life to be withheld from their servants and labourers, not caring whether the poor can live by their work or no. To make a man carry the sheaf and yet keep him hungry is worse, the witnesses agree, than muzzling the ox that treads out the corn, a cruelty the law of Deut. 25:4 itself forbade. The verse needs no interpretive quarrel to make its point; it stands as a study in the exact reversal of justice — nakedness in the midst of cloth, hunger in the midst of grain, the sheaf borne in by the very man it will never feed — and Job sets it down precisely because it is so visible and so unavenged.
11:
The forced labour moves from the harvest-field to the press-house, and the witnesses watch men crush out oil and wine they will never taste. The reformed John Gill will not read “within their walls” of the poor's own dwellings, as though they pressed their oil secretly for fear of its being taken; the labourers are within the walls of their rich masters, or rather among the rows of the olive-trees, where they gather the fruit and press out the oil at noon in the heat of the day, and yet are given nothing to quench their thirst. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as the plain sequel of all that has gone before: stripped of clothing and food, the poor are reduced to vassals, set to labour in the fields on scanty fare, or to tread the wine-presses of a produce from which they are not permitted so much as to slake their thirst.

John Wesley says the same in a sentence: the oil is made within the walls of the oppressors and for their use, and the treaders suffer thirst because they are not suffered to drink of the wine they make. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into the cry of James 5:4, that the hire of the labourers kept back cries out against the rich; these masters not only give no wages, though the labourer is worthy of his hire, but grudge even the meat and drink that would keep him at his task, not caring whether their servants can live by their labour or no, and forgetting that they themselves have a Master in heaven.

The witnesses do not divide, and they let the tantalizing cruelty of the picture speak for itself. There is a peculiar sharpness in it, which Gill catches in the detail that the labourers press the oil at noon, in the very heat of the day, and are given nothing to slake them: to stand thirsting among the wine-vats, to tread out the very juice one may not taste, is a torment more refined than open robbery, and it is inflicted not in the heat of a raid but in the settled routine of an estate. Job's argument gathers weight with every such instance — that a whole economy of quiet extortion runs on unchecked, its authors fed to the full while those who feed them go thirsty, and heaven, for all the friends' confident doctrine, sends down no sudden stroke to right it.
12:
The oppression that has stalked the open country now rises as a groan out of the streets, and the witnesses gather at the hardest words of the chapter: “Men groan from out of the city, and the soul of the wounded crieth out: yet God layeth not folly to them.” The reformed John Gill marks that the cruelty is no longer hidden in obscure corners but done openly in the cities, where the courts of justice sit, and yet in defiance of law and justice; there, if anywhere, the wronged should find redress, and there the oppressors fear neither the restraints of law nor the censure of their neighbours. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the city beside the country he has just surveyed: in the towns the rich merchants and traders are as cruel to their poor debtors as the landlords are to their tenants, and the oppressed groan and cry out like wounded men, unable to ease or help themselves against creditors inexorable and deaf to their groans.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke brings the misery indoors with a scene from his own experience, of a poor London district where he found each dwelling crowded with the sick and the dead, sixty souls under a single roof, groaning under evils he traces to ruthless landlords and to the taxation and ruin of unnecessary wars; the soul of the wounded, wounded in spirit and afflicted in body, cries out to God and man for help. On the closing clause he offers three renderings without choosing: that God does not impute the poor's calamities to their own folly; or, with the Vulgate, that he will not leave these disorders unpunished; or that he does not for the present attend to their prayers — the very point, Clarke says, that Job is pressing against his friends, that God does not hastily punish every evil work.

So a genuine divide runs through the last clause. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch take “God layeth not folly to them” of the oppressors — that he charges the wrongdoers with no folly, that is, sends no swift reckoning — and John Wesley agrees flatly, “yet God doth not punish them.” Gill hovers over the same sense of impunity, while Clarke keeps the alternative open that the “them” are the sufferers, and the clause a lament that their prayers seem unheard. The witnesses do not resolve the ambiguity, and Job does not mean them to: whichever way the words are turned, they land on the scandal that governs the chapter — the visible, audible, undeniable groan of the wronged, and the silence of heaven that follows it.
13:
Job turns from oppression done in the daylight to a darker company who “rebel against the light,” and the witnesses divide at once over what that light is. The reformed John Gill takes it morally: the light of nature, against which these men act in the teeth of their own consciences; or the light of the law, as the Targum has it; or God himself, who is light, and in whom is no darkness at all — for every sin is a rebellion against God and an act of hostility to him. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it the same way, as the light both of reason and conscience and of the divine revelation then in good measure imparted, adding that “they know not the ways thereof” means they do not approve, or love, or choose them. Adam Clarke joins the two lights, of God in the conscience and of God in his word, and describes men who will not learn their duty and, if ever brought to a better mind, speedily relapse, steady only in cruelty and mischief.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds both senses open and turns the ambiguity into the very theme of the passage. Some understand it figuratively, that they sin against the light of nature and conscience; others literally, that they have the daylight and choose the night as the fittest season for their wickedness. Sinful works are therefore called works of darkness, for he that does evil hates the light (John 3:20), and forgets that there is no darkness where the workers of iniquity may hide from God's eye (ch. 34:22). These, Henry says, are the worst of sinners, who sin wilfully against their own convictions and with a great deal of plot and contrivance.

The grammatical-historical witnesses press the wording. Keil and Delitzsch mark a new turn beginning here, “others are those that rebel against the light,” whose general character is that they shun it; the murderer, adulterer, and thief of the following verses are but this class in particular. Charles Ellicott finds the expression “very remarkable,” seeming to anticipate the teaching of St. John, and points ahead to the Word who was the true light of John 1:9. So the debate stands unresolved and fruitful: the light against which these men rebel is at once the moral light of conscience and revelation and the physical light of day they flee from — and the witnesses let the double sense enrich rather than embarrass the verse, since the men who hate the one are precisely the men who hide from the other.
14:
The first of the light-haters to be named is the murderer, and the witnesses take his trade at dawn as the type of a wickedness that works in the twilight of the day. The reformed John Gill sets the hour exactly: the murderer rises with the first light of morning, before the sun is up, when the early traveller is abroad on the road and the poor labourer goes forth to his work, and lies in wait to rob and kill them. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line “the murderer riseth up at dawn, he slayeth the sufferer and the poor, and in the night he acteth like a thief,” so that the same man is a highwayman by day and a housebreaker by dark, and Charles Ellicott observes that the very order of these crimes — murder, then adultery, then theft — follows the order of the Decalogue, which he takes as suggestive of the writer's acquaintance with it.

A quiet difference opens over the words “the poor and needy.” Gill and Keil and Delitzsch read them of the victim, the humble traveller cut down for the little he carries; the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, following Mr. Good's rendering “poor and needy, he sheddeth blood,” refers them rather to the murderer himself, a man driven by poverty and distress to the highway, who adds murder to robbery for fear of being taken. Either way the line runs from bad to worse, and Clarke presses the misery of a wretch who, having turned highwayman by day, becomes a footpad or housebreaker by night, going on from sin to sin.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the pathos of the prey and the horror of the appetite together. The murderer rises with the light to kill poor travellers going to market with a little money or goods; and though the game is so small that they are truly to be called poor and needy, he will both take his neighbour's life and venture his own for it, killing at last for killing's sake, thirsting more for blood than for booty. See, Henry adds, what care and pains wicked men take to compass their designs, and let it shame our slothfulness in doing good. John Wesley states the cruelty in a line: where the murderer finds nothing to satisfy his covetousness, he exercises his cruelty instead. The witnesses do not divide over the deed, only over whose poverty the verse names — the slain man's, or the slayer's.
15:
“The eye also of the adulterer waiteth for the twilight” — and the witnesses fasten, as the verse does, on the watching eye and the disguised face. The reformed John Gill is careful that it is the twilight of evening, not of morning, that the adulterer awaits, for he would have the whole night before him; he watches with impatience for the close of day and takes the first cover of darkness to set out on his errand. The eye is singled out, Gill notes, not only because it discerns the failing light but because it is itself the inlet to the sin, the leader and caterer and nourisher of it, the very eye that the apostle Peter says is full of adultery in 2 Pet. 2:14.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills out the whole nocturnal adventure. The adulterer has made his assignation and marked the house of the woman into whose favour he has crept; he waits impatiently for the dusk, and then goes forth with his face muffled and disguised, and spends a criminal night; but when the morning dawns it is to him as the shadow of death, lest he be detected before he can reach his own door, and if he is recognized coming away the terrors of death seize him, in dread of a sanguinary reckoning from the injured husband. So the disguise, Clarke observes, is the outward mark of an inward fear that dogs the sin from its beginning.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the moral from the secrecy. The unclean and wanton eyes wait for the twilight, as the adulteress herself did in Prov. 7:9; adultery hides its head for shame, so that even the most impudent do what they can to conceal it — if not chastely, yet cautiously — and it hides for fear too, knowing that jealousy is the rage of a husband who will not spare in the day of vengeance (Prov. 6:34-35). See, Henry says, what pains men take to make provision for the flesh, pains to compass and then to conceal what will be death and hell at last, when less pains would serve to mortify the flesh and end in life; let the sinner but change his heart, and he need not disguise his face, but may lift it up without spot. The witnesses do not divide; they read the veiled face as the confession the adulterer will not make aloud — that his deed cannot bear the light of day, nor, though he forgets it, escape the eye that needs none.
16:
The third of the night's trades is burglary, and the witnesses work at both the picture and a question of whom the verse describes. The reformed John Gill considers whether the diggers-through be the adulterers just named, breaking in by night to the women whose houses they have marked; but he thinks such a course neither safe nor necessary, and reads the verse rather of the thief and his fellows, the housebreakers who in the daytime observe which dwellings are full of money, plate, and rich goods, mark the easiest way in, and perhaps set a private sign upon them, and then break through the walls, doors, or windows in the dark. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes the subject to be the robber, who, having had the adulterer brought in beside him as one that likewise acts his sin by night, now returns to the housebreaker's proper work.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott holds the alternatives together. “Which they had marked for themselves in the daytime” may instead be rendered that they “seal up,” or shut, themselves in by day, keeping close until dark; and he notes the eastern custom by which such men sought access to the harem in female attire, a hint that the burglar and the adulterer are not always distinct. The clause “they know not the light,” he adds, when set beside its use in v.13, shows the strikingly different force the same expression can carry — there a moral rebellion against the light, here the literal night-creature's ignorance of day. Keil and Delitzsch expound the whole as the handiwork of a band of thieves who break into houses in the dark and shut themselves up by day, wanting nothing to do with the light.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the three night-sinners into one observation of law and conscience. These house-breakers mark the avenues of a dwelling in the day and dig through in the night, when the good man of the house knows not what hour the thief will come and lies exposed asleep, as in Luke 12:39; for which reason, Henry notes, the law counts burglary a felony without benefit of clergy. The witnesses do not finally divide. Whether the digger be thief or adulterer, they agree that the darkness he courts is chosen, a deliberate flight from the light he hates, and that the very pains he takes to hide betray a conscience that already knows itself watched.
17:
“The morning is to them even as the shadow of death” — and the witnesses read this closing line of the passage as the secret punishment already at work in the light-haters' own breasts. The reformed John Gill notes that the daybreak, welcome to honest men, is to these as disagreeable and terrible as the thickest darkness can be to others; the word, he says, is better rendered “alike” or “together” than “even,” so that the morning is to the murderer, thief, adulterer, and housebreaker equally as the shadow of death — for they love darkness rather than light. John Wesley puts it in three words: to them the morning is “terrible and hateful.”

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the thought into the next clause, rendering that the depth of night is to such men as the dawn of morning, for they are at home in its terrors and know it as their working day; the very things that appal others are their element. Their reading turns the verse into a portrait of natures so inverted that light and dark have changed places, and what should be the hour of security has become the hour of dread. Gill's rendering, that the morning is to them “alike” or “together” as the shadow of death, points the same way: not merely that daybreak is unwelcome, but that for the whole company of them — murderer, thief, adulterer, and housebreaker together — it wears the very face of death, because the light they have fled all night must at last find them out.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes that dread the point, and finds in it a present, secret judgment on the sinner. The light of day, he says, is a terror to bad people; they curse the sun, not as the Moors for its scorching, but because it discovers them, and if any man knows them their consciences fly in their faces and they stand in the terrors of the shadow of death. See here, Henry urges, the misery of sinners, exposed to continual frights, and their folly too — that they are afraid of coming under the eye of men, yet have no dread of God's eye, which is always upon them, and are not afraid to do the very things they are so terrified to be known to do. Shame came in with sin, and everlasting shame is at the end of it. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the man who has fled the light all night is overtaken by his own terror at dawn, so that the punishment the friends looked for from without has begun already within, in a heart that finds the daylight itself its accuser.
18:
With the eighteenth verse the argument turns, and the witnesses divide more widely here than anywhere in the chapter, for it is not clear whether Job still describes the wicked's way of life or begins to speak of his end. The reformed John Gill records the reading that takes “swift as the waters” of yet another class of malefactors, pirates and sea-robbers who choose the swiftest vessels for their prey; but he doubts whether such existed so early, and notes Schultens's guess that Sodomites are meant, men profuse in lust who have no regard to the honest labour of the vineyard. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives both the sea-robber reading, after bishop Patrick — privateers cruising in fast ships, whose portion is cursed and who despise the way of the vineyards as poor and unprofitable — and the alternative, that these are the light-hating sinners still, who when discovered get away as fast as running water and lurk not in the cultivated vineyards but in some cursed and desolate portion no one looks after.

The grammatical-historical witnesses read it of swift flight rather than a new trade. Charles Ellicott would not take the phrase as a comparison at all, but render that each of these rebels against the light is swift to make his escape over the face of the waters; their portion is cursed, that is, men give it an evil name, and he “turneth not the way of the vineyards,” the frequented and cultivated ground, but chooses lone and rugged paths. Keil and Delitzsch make the point of the simile the swiftness of a light thing hurried along on the surface of the current and scarcely seen, comparing the fleeting days of ch. 9:26. Adam Clarke keeps close to the letter, “light is he on the face of the waters,” and reads the last clause of vineyards that no longer flourish, the labour of the vintage failing.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley alone gives the verse the turn the rest of the chapter will follow: the wicked man “is swift as the waters” in that he quickly passes away with all his glory, as the waters never stay in one place but are always hasting off; his portion is the estate he leaves behind, and he shall never more see or enjoy his vineyards. So the debate is real and unresolved — whether the verse paints a new band of sea-rovers, or the quick escape of the criminal over the water, or the transitory rushing-away of the wicked toward his grave. The witnesses do not force agreement; but Wesley's reading quietly opens the door through which the chapter now passes, from the impunity of the wicked to their swift and certain end.
19:
“Drought and heat consume the snow waters: so doth the grave those which have sinned” — and the witnesses hear in the simile the first plain word of the wicked's disappearance. The reformed John Gill keeps the picture simple: as drought and heat melt the snow into water and then dry up that water, easily, quickly, and all at once, so are sinners snatched away to the grave. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enlarges the image to the failing of the great cisterns and tanks that the melted snow of the mountains had filled for the year's irrigation, now exhausted by the long heat, so that succour is cut off from every quarter; and on the terse second clause — in the Hebrew but two words, sheol chatau — he notes that sheol means any deep pit as well as the grave, and follows Mr. Good's rendering “they fall to their lowest depth,” the sinners going down as the deepest tank drains dry.

The grammatical-historical witnesses give the verse its place in the argument. Keil and Delitzsch render “drought, also heat, snatch away snow water — so doth Sheol those who have sinned,” and read it as the opening of Job's account of how the ungodly, feared in life, are yet carried off; the following lines will show how little they were loved once they are gone. Charles Ellicott observes that Job had already spoken of the sudden death of the wicked as a kind of blessing in ch. 21:13, an easy vanishing compared with the lingering torture he himself was made to undergo.

Beneath the shared image runs the delicate question of Job's drift. Is the snow-water's vanishing a comfort or a complaint? For the friends it would prove the certain doom of sinners; for Job, as Ellicott hints, it is rather the mark of how gently the wicked are taken, melting quietly away where he is left to suffer on. Gill keeps the picture deliberately simple — the snow melts to water and the water is dried up, easily, quickly, and all at once — and that very ease is the sting, for there is nothing here of the lingering, exemplary punishment the friends had promised. The witnesses do not force the matter to a debate, but they feel the double edge: the same verse that concedes the wicked's mortality also protests the ease of it, and Job wields the concession as much against his friends' theology as for it, since a death so painless is no visible stroke of judgment at all.
20:
The wicked man's memory is the next thing to perish, and the witnesses read the twentieth verse as the quiet erasure of a life: “the womb shall forget him; the worm shall feed sweetly on him.” The reformed John Gill canvasses whose womb it is that forgets — the mother that bore him, or the wife by whom he had children, or a once-affectionate friend, who now, whether from the shame of his life or the ease of his death, care not to speak of him but bury him in oblivion; or else the womb of the earth in which he lies forgotten; or even, since the word carries the sense of mercy, God himself, who has no favour for such men and remembers them no more in grace. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes on that last shade: the word rechem means compassion, so that “mercy shall be unmindful of him” — and how dreadful a state, he cries, when mercy itself forgets a man; the worm feeds sweetly on him, and the Chaldee turns it that the cruel who would not pity the poor shall themselves be sweet to the worms.

On the last clause, “wickedness shall be broken as a tree,” the witnesses weigh a further nicety. Clarke reads him a rotten and decayed tree, easily broken to pieces, but records Mr. Good's ingenious turn, that if the word for wickedness be kin to the word for a shoot or sucker, the line might mean the shoot broken off as from a tree. John Wesley keeps it plainer: the wicked man is broken to pieces, or violently broken down, like a tree that once felled never grows again.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott raises the real question of mood. Some understand the whole verse not as what does befall the wicked but as what ought to — “his own mother should forget him, the worm should feed sweetly on him, he should be no more remembered, and then unrighteousness would be broken as a tree” — a wish for justice rather than a report of it. So the debate is genuine, though softly held: whether Job here describes the actual oblivion into which the wicked sink, easy and unavenged, or voices what their end by rights should be. The witnesses do not divide over the pathos of the forgetting; they part only over whether it is fact or longing, and Job, in the ambiguity, keeps both his grief and his complaint alive.
21:
Job returns to the wicked man's dealings with the helpless, and the witnesses meet a real crux in the verb, for it is not settled whether he wrongs the barren or befriends her. The reformed John Gill takes “he evil entreateth the barren that beareth not” of a man who uses his wife ill because she is childless, upbraiding and afflicting her; or, since the word can mean to associate with, of one who consorts with the barren and with harlots and wastes his substance among them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verb the other way entirely, “he feedeth the barren,” as the Vulgate has it, so that the reproach lies in the contrast: he has been kind to the childless woman who might serve his turn, but has done no good to the widow, showing no mercy to her because she is old or infirm and of no use to his purpose.

John Wesley keeps to the harsher rendering and gives the reason it bites: barrenness was esteemed a curse and a reproach, so that to entreat the barren evilly is to add affliction to the afflicted, taunting a woman for the very grief she cannot help. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it so, and likens the cruelty to Peninnah's vexing of Hannah, upbraiding the childless on purpose to make them fret; the barren, like the fatherless, are in some degree helpless, wanting the arrows in the quiver that others have to plead with their enemies in the gate (Ps. 127:5), and it is the same barbarity to hurt the widow, to whom we ought rather to do good — for not to do good, when it is in our power, is itself to do hurt.

So the witnesses hold two opposite construals of the line without coming to blows over it. On Gill, Wesley, and Henry's reading the wicked man torments a woman for her barrenness and denies the widow all kindness — a double cruelty to two sorts of the defenceless. On Clarke's, the sting is a partiality: kindness lavished where it may profit, and mercy withheld where it cannot. Either way the verse fastens on the same character, a man whose treatment of the weakest is governed by nothing but his own advantage; and either way it deepens Job's charge, that such a man goes on unpunished while heaven looks the other way. It is, Henry adds, no small part of the wickedness that it is directed at those least able to resist — the childless, the widowed, the defenceless — from whom nothing is to be feared and to whom, therefore, nothing is shown.
22:
The wicked man's reach now extends even to the strong, and the witnesses divide three ways over a verse whose very subject is in doubt. The reformed John Gill reads “he draweth also the mighty with his power” of the oppressor himself, who not only tramples the weak but by superior force draws even the powerful into his party, or ensnares them by power and policy as he catches the poor in his net, and makes a prey of them and their substance; he rises up in his violence, and no man is sure of his life before him. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it the same way and paints the terror of such a man: by inuring himself to cruelty he becomes the terror of the mighty in the land of the living, drawing them into a snare with his power, so that in his mad fits the greatest cannot stand before him, his hand against every man and every man's hand against him, after the manner of Ishmael in Gen. 16:12.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes the line by Calmet's very different rendering, that the tyrant “draws with him guards for his defence; he raises himself up, and does not feel assured of his life” — an admirable picture, he says, of a despot's inward terror, who even in the midst of his bodyguard is afraid and can trust no one; without are fightings, within are fears. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott keeps to the tyrant who draws others by influence and example into his own courses, and reads “he riseth up, and no man is sure of his life” of men wholly under his sway.

But Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, turn the verse clean around by making God its subject: “He preserveth the mighty by his strength; such an one riseth again, though he despaired of life.” On their reading it is not the tyrant overpowering the strong but the LORD sustaining the wicked mighty, raising up again the very man who had given himself up for lost — a sovereign forbearance that prolongs the oppressor rather than a violence that fells his rivals. So the debate is genuine and unresolved: whether the mighty man drags others down by his power, or lives in dread amid his own guards, or is himself upheld and revived by the God who bears with him. The witnesses do not reconcile the three; and the last, read into Job's mouth, sharpens his complaint to its keenest, that the hand which should strike the oppressor seems rather to hold him up.
23:
The wicked man's security is the theme of the twenty-third verse, and the witnesses differ over whose watching eye keeps him. The reformed John Gill reads “though it be given him to be in safety” as of God's own hand: it is God who gives the wicked to be in safety despite all his wickedness, for even bad men are often preserved from the depredations of others and left to dwell secure and confident; “yet his eyes are upon their ways,” that is, God's eyes, so that the same providence which grants the respite also keeps the account. John Wesley reads it exactly so — God gives them strange successes, yet sees and observes all their ways, and will in due time punish them.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets aside the Vulgate's turn, that God gave the man space for repentance which he abused through pride, as not faithful to the original, and renders the verse instead of the suspicious tyrant of the preceding line: God, or rather the man, gives him the guards for his security, and he leans upon them, yet his own eyes are upon their ways, watching his bodyguard continually lest they plot his destruction — again the true picture of an eastern despot, without are fightings, within are fears. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gives both constructions their due: on the one hand the great tyrant grants his followers their tribute or their footing that he may be secure and stable, and his eyes are on their ways; on the other, the subject of “he giveth him to be in security” may well be God, whose eyes are on the ways of them all, and this, Ellicott allows, makes very good sense.

Keil and Delitzsch keep the reading of a divine forbearance, rendering “he giveth him rest, and he is sustained, and his eyes are over their ways,” so that God upholds the wicked and yet never loses sight of him. So a genuine divide runs through the verse: are the watching eyes God's, marking the ways of men he has for a season let alone, or the tyrant's, fixed in distrust upon the guards he dare not trust? The witnesses do not settle it, but the two readings meet in a single irony — that whether it be heaven's patient gaze or a despot's sleepless suspicion, the man given to be “in safety” is never truly safe, being watched from above even as he watches, in fear, all around him.
24:
Now at last the wicked are brought down, and the witnesses read the twenty-fourth verse as the measured close of their prosperity: “they are exalted for a little while, but are gone and brought low.” The reformed John Gill dwells on the brevity that the words insist on — exalted to seats of honour, to wealth and profit and the esteem of men, but only “for a little while,” this life at its longest being short as a vapour; and he would even join the phrase to what follows, “a little while, and they are gone,” so that the height and the fall are named almost in one breath. Gill notes, too, how nearly this comes to Zophar's sentiment, that the triumphing of the wicked is short — as though Job, pressed to the point, will grant the friends the ending while denying them the plain and present justice they claim.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the picture with a harder line: such tyrants are exalted for a time, for God puts down one and raises up another, but he turns his hand and they are gone, removed by his justice as all of their kind have been; time and judgment mow them down like grass and crop them like ripe ears of corn. And he adds the grim observation of experience, that few tyrants leave the world by a natural death, but most by a violent one, all eastern history being full of the fact. John Wesley reads “taken out of the way as all other” to mean that they can no more prevent or delay their death than the meanest men in the world, and “cut off as the tops of the ears of corn” of a life reaped in its greatest height and maturity.

Keil and Delitzsch render the whole to the same effect — “they are exalted a little while, then they are no more, and they are sunken away, snatched away like all others, and as the top of the stalk they are cut off” — laying the stress on the suddenness with which the feared man ceases to be. The witnesses do not divide over the end, but they weigh its bearing carefully. The fall is real, yet it is quiet and shared, a being gathered like corn with all other men rather than singled out for a public vengeance; and that, for Job, is the very edge of the matter — that the wicked come down at last only as every man comes down, in death, and not before, so that their long exaltation stands unrebuked to the end.
25:
Job closes his speech as a man closes a case, staking the whole of it on the plain facts he has laid down: “and if it be not so now, who will make me a liar, and make my speech nothing worth?” The reformed John Gill reads the challenge as resting on all that has gone before — if it be not so, that men of such wicked lives do prosper in the world, increase in riches, pass through it with impunity, and die quietly in the full possession of their honour and wealth, then let it be disproved. The weight of the appeal, Gill implies, is that Job has described nothing but what all the world may see; he does not argue from a hidden principle but points to the open course of events and dares any man to deny it.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the challenge squarely against the friends' doctrine. They had maintained that the righteous are so distinguished in God's approval that they always live in prosperity and die in peace, and that a reputed good man fallen into adversity is thereby unmasked as a secret sinner; on this ground they had charged Job with hypocrisy, his very afflictions being taken for proof of heinous sin. Job repels the whole scheme by appeal to fact, where the bad are demonstrably bad and yet in prosperity, and the good demonstrably good and yet in adversity, and defies his friends to show one flaw in the argument. It is a pity, Clarke adds, that none of them could hit on the middle way — that the wicked may prosper and yet be miserable in his soul, and the righteous be afflicted and yet happy in his God — for in that deeper sense God's ways are always equal.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the last words the calm of a man willing to be examined. Let those who can, he says, prove Job's discourse either false in itself, and so prove him a liar, or foreign and nothing to the purpose, and so prove his speech frivolous; but those who speak the words of truth and soberness need not fear having what they say brought to the test, and can cheerfully submit it to a fair trial. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sums up the standoff: Job also has his facts, as ready and as incontrovertible as those of his friends, and yet irreconcilable with theirs. The witnesses do not divide. They leave Job resting his case not on eloquence but on evidence, certain that the plain and painful truth he has told about the prosperity of the wicked will bear any honest scrutiny — and that the burden of disproof, if there be any, lies wholly upon the men who have come to comfort him.
